opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one of the parts we're still actively exploring. Let me share how I think about it right now.

The starting intuition comes from the brain. Different parts of the brain operate at different frequencies, like gamma, beta, and theta waves, and you can think of each frequency as a level of abstraction. Some information needs to be absorbed very quickly and is local to the current context. Other information is more persistent and should change slowly, because it's knowledge you've consolidated over a long time. So in what we call the continuum memory system, instead of the classic dichotomy of attention as short-term memory and MLPs as long-term memory, we have a spectrum of MLP blocks, each updating at its own frequency.

On update frequency, the simplest way to think about it is chunk size: how many tokens does a block see before it updates its parameters? A high-frequency block might update every few tokens or every small chunk, so it's very adaptive and captures local patterns. A low-frequency block might update only every few thousand tokens, or barely at all at test time, so it behaves more like the persistent knowledge you got from pre-training. In practice we've found that a roughly geometric spacing works well, where each level is slower than the previous by a constant factor. That gives you coverage across timescales without lots of redundant levels that do the same thing.

On dimensions, my intuition, and the experiments support it, is that slower levels should generally have more capacity. They're supposed to compress and store a lot of information over a long horizon, so they need more parameters. The fast levels hold less at any moment, because they're constantly overwritten, so they can be smaller. Making them smaller also helps efficiency, since those are the ones you update most often. So there's a nice alignment there: the expensive updates happen rarely on the big blocks, and the cheap updates happen frequently on the small ones.

There's also a practical side. You can initialize the slower levels from a pre-trained model's MLP blocks, which means you don't have to retrain everything from scratch to get this multi-timescale behavior. The pre-trained weights already act like the slowest memory, and you add faster levels on top.

I'd be honest, though: right now these are mostly design choices guided by intuition and ablations, not something we derive from first principles. A really exciting direction is making the frequencies themselves learnable or data-dependent, so the model decides how often each level should update based on how surprising or novel the incoming data is. That's closer to how I think memory consolidation actually works, and I think that's where a lot of the future gains will come from.

r001.rationale: It says high-frequency blocks are more adaptive and capture local patterns, while slower update rates suit less adaptive behavior.

r002.rationale: It links low-frequency updates to persistent knowledge and describes slower blocks as storing information over a long horizon.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of the questions we spent the most time on, and I'll say upfront that part of the answer is still empirical, we don't have a closed-form rule for it yet.

The way I think about it starts from the motivation. The reason you want blocks updating at different rates in the first place is that you want a kind of continuum of memory. You have the fastest level, which is basically the attention or the recurrent state, updating every token. Then you want something that updates every, say, sixteen tokens, something every few hundred, something every few thousand, and so on. Each level is supposed to abstract the level below it. So the slower block is not seeing raw tokens, it's seeing a compressed summary of what the faster block has accumulated, and it decides what's worth consolidating.

Once you frame it that way, the frequency question becomes: how far apart should those levels be? And what we found is that you want roughly geometric spacing. If two levels are too close, like one updates every eight tokens and the next every sixteen, they end up learning almost the same thing and you're just wasting parameters. If they're too far apart, the slow block gets so few gradient steps during a context that it barely moves, and it effectively becomes frozen weights. So in practice we pick a base chunk size, often driven by hardware, what gives you an efficient parallel scan or matmul, and then multiply by a fairly large factor, four to sixteen, between levels. The exact factor matters less than keeping the ratio consistent across levels.

The dimension question is a bit more subtle, and this is where I think intuitions from classical memory systems are useful. The fast level sees a lot of information but doesn't need to retain it, so it can be relatively small, it's okay if it gets overwritten. The slow level sees very little information per update, but each thing it stores needs to persist for a long time and represent something more abstract, so you actually want more capacity there, or at least more expressive capacity, meaning deeper MLPs rather than just wider ones. We found depth matters more than width for the slow blocks. A two or three layer MLP as the memory module was consistently better than a single wide linear map at the same parameter count, and that gap grew as the update frequency decreased.

There's also a compute budget argument that falls out naturally. A block that updates every thousand tokens is only doing its inner-loop update a thousandth as often, so you can afford to make it much larger for essentially free in terms of training throughput. So in a sense the slow blocks are where you can hide a lot of parameters without paying for them on every token.

The thing I'm still not satisfied with is that all of this is set by hand. Ideally the model would learn when to update, not just how much. We have some early versions of that, where the update is gated by a surprise signal so the block only writes when something unexpected happens, and that partially replaces the fixed frequency with a data-dependent one. But making that stable at scale is still an open problem, and I think it's one of the more interesting directions right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses update rates and memory levels, but does not say that the chosen frequency depends on the desired degree of model adaptivity.

r002.rationale: It says different update rates create a continuum of memory, with slower blocks consolidating summaries and storing information that persists longer.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as two coupled choices: how much capacity you give a block, and how quickly you allow that capacity to change. A larger block can represent more information, but if you update it frequently, you also pay more computation. So I wouldn’t choose the dimensions independently of the update schedule.

The intuition is that different parts of the model should operate on different timescales. Some information is very specific to what you’re processing right now, and you want a component that can adapt quickly. Other structure persists across many inputs, so you want a component that changes more slowly. Updating everything at the same rate doesn’t necessarily match that distinction.

But that intuition doesn’t give you a unique configuration. I’d treat the dimensions and frequencies as design choices to explore under a fixed compute budget. Does adding capacity at a particular timescale improve performance? Does updating that block more frequently actually help, or are you spending computation without gaining much? Ultimately, the useful allocation depends on the task and the timescales in the data.

r001.rationale: It says some information should adapt quickly, while other information should change more slowly, tying update frequency to the desired adaptivity.

r002.rationale: It describes structure that persists across many inputs and says its component should change more slowly, communicating a slower update rate for persistent information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about those as two related design choices: how much capacity you give a block, and over what timescale you want it to learn. A block that updates frequently can adapt to the immediate context, while a slower block can retain information across a longer horizon. You want enough capacity at each level to capture the structure that is useful at that timescale.

But I wouldn’t say there’s a universal rule that the faster block should be larger or smaller. Updating a large MLP frequently is expensive, so you have to balance adaptation against compute. And if a slow block is too small, it may become a bottleneck for the information you want to preserve.

A reasonable starting point is to space the update frequencies across different timescales, then vary the dimensions under a fixed compute budget. The important question is whether those levels are actually learning complementary things. Ultimately, I think choosing those dimensions and frequencies automatically is more interesting than treating them as architectural constants that we have to tune by hand.

r001.rationale: It says frequently updated blocks can adapt to immediate context, tying update frequency to the desired adaptivity.

r002.rationale: It says slower blocks retain information across a longer horizon, tying update frequency to persistent memory.
